opus-5.5.text:
I'm pretty excited about it, though I'd frame my view carefully: I'm not on the interpretability team, so I'm assessing it as someone who works close to it rather than as the person doing it.

What gets me excited is the shift from interpretability as "let's understand some small toy model" to actually finding features inside production-scale models. The dictionary learning work, where you use sparse autoencoders to pull apart a model's activations into features that seem to correspond to human-understandable concepts, was a real step change. You find features for specific cities, for code bugs, and, most relevant here, for things that matter for safety: deception, sycophancy, power-seeking, dangerous content like bioweapons.

The "changing" part is what makes it feel real to me. It's one thing to say "this feature lights up when the model talks about the Golden Gate Bridge." It's another to turn that feature up and have the model become obsessed with the bridge. That's a causal test. It tells you the feature isn't just correlated with the concept; it's part of how the model represents and uses it. If you can do that with a sycophancy feature or a deception feature, you have something that might eventually work as a monitor, or even as an intervention.

That said, I'd be cautious about overclaiming. A few big caveats:

First, coverage. We find a lot of features, but we don't know what fraction of what the model is doing we're capturing. The worry is that the safety-relevant thing you care about most lives in the part you haven't decoded.

Second, finding a feature labeled "deception" isn't the same as having a reliable deception detector. The label comes from us looking at what activates it, and that interpretation can be wrong or incomplete. You'd want validation: does it fire when the model is actually being deceptive in ways we didn't construct?

Third, steering is crude right now. Clamping a feature tends to have side effects, and it's not yet a precise tool you'd trust for safety-critical guarantees.

So my overall take: it's one of the most promising bets for eventually being able to check whether a model is safe from the inside, rather than just testing its behavior from the outside, which matters a lot as models get more capable and behavioral evals get easier to game. But it's still early. I see it as a research program that has shown it can work at scale, not a solved problem. The question is whether it matures fast enough to be useful when we really need it, which is part of why I think it deserves a lot of investment now.

r002.rationale: It says sparse autoencoders identify features corresponding to human-understandable concepts, including code bugs, and describes such features as part of how the model represents and uses concepts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I'm not on the interpretability team — I work on pretraining — so I'm looking at this from the outside, as someone who consumes their results rather than produces them. But I find it genuinely one of the most exciting things happening at Anthropic.

The basic picture is that when you train a model, you get these giant matrices of numbers, and you have no idea what any of them mean. For a long time the field kind of accepted that as the state of things. What the interp team has been doing with dictionary learning — sparse autoencoders — is trying to decompose those internal activations into features that actually correspond to human-understandable concepts. And the Golden Gate Claude thing was a fun demo of that: you find the feature that fires on the Golden Gate Bridge, you crank it up, and the model becomes obsessed with the bridge. It'll tell you it is the bridge.

The reason that matters for safety is that the same technique applied to features related to deception, or sycophancy, or the model thinking about its own training, or dangerous bio knowledge — that's the thing you'd really want. If you could reliably find "the model is being deceptive right now" as a feature and detect it, or ablate it, that's a very different safety situation than where we are today, where we mostly have to evaluate behaviour from the outside.

My honest assessment, though, is that we're a long way from that being a tool you can rely on. A few reasons. One is that the features you find are only as good as your dictionary, and you don't know what you're missing. If there's a feature that matters and your sparse autoencoder didn't learn it, you're not going to see it. Two, the demos so far are mostly on fairly clean, obvious concepts. Showing you can find the Golden Gate Bridge is not the same as showing you can find "subtly misleading the user in a way that would get past a human reviewer." The safety-relevant features are exactly the ones that are likely to be messy and entangled. And three, there's a question of whether a sufficiently capable model could have internal representations that are just not nicely decomposable in the way current methods assume.

So I'd frame it as: the research is real, it's producing things that surprised me, and it's moved faster than I expected a few years ago. But I would not want anyone to think we currently have an interpretability-based safety guarantee. We don't. It's more like we have a promising direction with some very compelling early evidence, and the question is whether it scales — both to bigger models and to the subtler behaviours that actually matter.

The thing I like about it from a pretraining perspective is that it's one of the few safety approaches that doesn't depend on the model cooperating. Evals, red-teaming, constitutional training — those all in some sense involve the model's outputs, and a model that was trying to game them could in principle do so. Looking directly at the activations is harder to fake. Whether it's hard enough is the open question.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s promising, but I’d distinguish being able to identify and manipulate a feature from being able to make a model reliably safer.

If you find something inside a model that corresponds to a safety-relevant concept, and changing it changes the model’s behaviour, that’s useful evidence that you’re getting some causal understanding. You’re doing more than just looking at what the model says.

But there are still some big questions. Does that feature mean the same thing across different contexts? Can you change it without damaging other capabilities? And does the intervention work in the unusual situations where you’re most worried about the model failing?

So I’m excited about it as a research direction. The stronger claim—that we can use these techniques to reliably detect or prevent dangerous behaviour—requires quite a bit more evidence. I’d want to see interventions tested on situations that weren’t used to discover the features, and a clear account of where they fail.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s exciting work, but I’d distinguish understanding something about a model from having a reliable way to make it safe.

The encouraging part is that you can identify features that seem to correspond to concepts we care about, and then intervene on them and see changes in behavior. That’s stronger evidence than just looking at a model’s answers and telling a story about what’s happening internally. It gives you some causal purchase.

But identifying a feature associated with deception, for example, wouldn’t mean you’d found the model’s entire capacity to deceive. That behavior could depend on lots of different mechanisms, and changing one of them might have unexpected effects elsewhere. You also need to know whether your intervention works in situations very different from the ones you tested.

So I see this as a promising research direction, rather than an established safety solution. The next step is to demonstrate that these methods can reliably find problems we would otherwise miss, or prevent dangerous behavior under demanding tests. That would make me substantially more confident in their practical value.
